title: Landscape and design factors influencing the concentration and retention of chemical pollutants in urban stormwater control ponds
content:
Abstract
Stormwater control ponds are widespread in the urban landscape as a means of collecting rainfall-driven runoff. Because of their urban and suburban locations they are easily accessible to humans and their pets. Polluted stormwater ponds can be both ecosystem and human health hazards. As such, the sediments of 20 urban and suburban wet detention ponds on the US southeast Coastal Plain were analyzed for primary pollutant metals, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) and labile and refractory phosphorus (P) during 2022. These ponds drain into the upper reaches of estuarine creeks, which are designated primary nursery areas for finfish and shellfish. However, the sediments of some ponds were highly polluted (especially with PAHs), thus the retention of pollutants in such ponds is desirable. Pollutant concentrations were tested against potential terrestrial source factors, and correlation analyses revealed that both total impervious watershed area and percent impervious coverage were correlated with concentrations of PAHs and labile P. Potential in-pond pollutant retention factors were likewise tested, and refractory P was inversely related to sediment grain size and positively related to sediment organic content. Sediment organic content was a highly significant factor controlling the concentration (i.e. retention) of metals and PAHs in the detention ponds. Sediment organic composition >15% appears to be a desirable pond management goal in retention of the pollutants within the pond rather than allowing them to pollute downstream waterscapes. Additionally, increased pond depth was also positively correlated with higher sediment metals concentrations, providing another pond construction and maintenance objective.
